spec.method: Stirred: stir gently with ice in a mixing glass, pour into the glass
spec.glass: Rocks glass (highball if served with ice)
spec.ice: None by default; if the guest asks for ice, pour into a highball glass with ice

origin.text: Fernand Petiot is said to have created it at Harry's New York Bar in Paris in 1921, then refined it at the St. Regis Hotel's King Cole Bar in New York in 1934. Sources disagree: New York's 21 Club credits comedian George Jessel (or bartender Henry Zbikiewicz) in the 1930s, and a 1939 newspaper column called it 'George Jessel's newest pick-me-up'.

origin.text: Its origin is unclear; it was originally called a 'champagne orange.' Paris Ritz bartender Frank Meier is sometimes credited, but his own 1934 book doesn't mark it as his invention, and it is closely related to the Buck's Fizz, which dates from about 1921.

spec.notes: IBA: historically a few drops of fresh lime juice were added to taste; 4 slices of fresh pineapple can be used instead of juice. 50 ml is about 1⅔ oz.

origin.text: The Caribe Hilton in San Juan, Puerto Rico credits bartender Ramón 'Monchito' Marrero with creating it in 1954. Sources disagree: Ricardo García at the same hotel claimed 1953, and Barrachina restaurant credits Ramón Portas Mingot in 1963. Puerto Rico made it the official drink in 1978.

origin.text: Victor J. Bergeron (Trader Vic) said he invented it in 1944 at Trader Vic's in Oakland, California, and brought it to Hawaii's hotels in 1953. Donn Beach (Don the Beachcomber) claimed he made it first in 1933, though a longtime colleague said Beach was only claiming it was based on his Q.B. Cooler.

spec.notes: IBA has no separate Tom Collins page. This is the IBA John Collins, whose page says: 'Use Old Tom Gin for Tom Collins.'

origin.text: The earliest published Tom Collins recipe appeared in Harry Johnson's 1882 bar manual, and Jerry Thomas's 1887 edition also included one. The name is disputed: historians link it to the 1874 'Have you seen Tom Collins?' hoax in New York, or to the earlier John Collins, said to be named after a headwaiter at Limmer's in London and later made with Old Tom gin.

spec.method: Stirred: stir vodka and coffee liqueur with ice, strain into the ice-filled glass, then carefully float the cream on top (lightly whip or shake the cream first)
spec.notes: IBA has no full White Russian spec; its Black Russian page (https://iba-world.com/iba-cocktail/black-russian/: 50 ml vodka, 20 ml coffee liqueur, old fashioned glass with ice) adds 'WHITE RUSSIAN – Float fresh cream on the top and stir in slowly', with no cream amount. Difford's spec used instead (it names Ketel One and Galliano Espresso as brands).

origin.text: It's the Black Russian (first seen in 1949) with cream added; who first added the cream is unknown. It first appeared in print in 1965 (Oakland Tribune, Nov 21, 1965) and became hugely popular after The Big Lebowski (1998).

spec.method: Built: pour warm black coffee into a preheated glass, add whiskey and at least 1 tsp sugar, stir until dissolved, then pour thick chilled cream over the back of a spoon held just above the surface so it floats
spec.notes: IBA: plain sugar can be replaced with sugar syrup. 50 ml is about 1⅔ oz.

origin.text: Joe Sheridan, head chef at the Foynes air base near today's Shannon Airport in Ireland, is credited with adding whiskey to the coffee of arriving passengers in 1942 or 1943. San Francisco Chronicle writer Stanton Delaplane brought it to the Buena Vista Cafe in San Francisco, which began serving it on November 10, 1952.

spec.method: Muddled and stirred: gently muddle mint with sugar and water in the cup, fill with cracked ice, add bourbon, stir until the cup frosts

origin.text: It began in the American South, probably in the 18th century; the earliest known mentions are from 1770 in Virginia. Churchill Downs has promoted it with the Kentucky Derby since 1938.
